items.title: Hackers Abuse Claude’s Official Website and Google Ads to Spread Malware
items.summary: Cybercriminals found a simple way to make a fake download page look trustworthy. Instead of registering a lookalike domain, they placed their lure on claude.ai, the official website of Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI assistant. The fake page carried Claude branding and offered what looked like easy steps to install a desktop app. The attackers also paid for Google Ads so these pages appeared near the top of search results. Anthropic never published these instructions, and the page had no installer. It told visitors to copy a command and paste it into Terminal on their Mac. Anyone who followed the steps installed Atomic macOS Stealer, known as AMOS, a program built to steal passwords, browser sessions, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive data. The malware can also replace the real Ledger and Trezor desktop apps with modified copies that ask for the wallet recovery phrase. Researchers at Gen Digital, including threat analysis engineer Vojtěch Moravec, identified these campaigns and described them in a Gen Digital’s full research report published on October 26, 2026. Gen’s team also found a second campaign that used the same method against Windows users, with different instructions and a different final payload. This shows the threat is not limited to one operating system. Hackers Abuse Claude’s Official Website and Google Ads Most phishing relies on small clues, such as a misspelled domain or a missing padlock. This campaign removed those clues. The fake “Download Claude” pages were user-generated content on claude.ai, delivered as either a Shared Chat or a public Artifact. Both are normal Claude sharing features. Claude shows a thin banner saying the content is user-generated and unverified, but the domain, padlock, and logo all look genuine. The malicious links carried Google Ads tracking parameters such as gclid and gad_campaignid, which confirms the attackers paid to promote them. Researchers also found several rotating Artifacts tied to two ad campaigns, so this was a funded, ongoing operation rather than a single case. MALICIOUS — the fake “Download Claude” page hosted as a claude.ai Artifact (Source – GenDigital) Cyber Security News reported on similar lures earlier in the year, in its coverage of fake Claude installer pages that also used sponsored search results. The lure depends on a technique called ClickFix, which asks the victim to run a command personally. The page shows a box titled “Install on macOS” with four steps: open Terminal, click Copy, paste, and press Enter. The copied command is scrambled, so the visitor sees only gibberish instead of a suspicious web address. Because the user runs it, many built-in defenses do not stop it. Earlier reports, including past ClickFix technique research , show how widely this pattern has spread. Windows Campaign, Wallet Theft, and Protection Tips The Windows version used an Artifact titled “Install Claude on Windows,” which told users to press Win + R, then Ctrl + V, then Enter. The pasted PowerShell command was malicious from its first character and displayed fake “verification” messages while it ran. It then reached GitHub and a github.io page to fetch the next stage, which carried an encrypted .NET payload. The whole attack, step by step (Source – GenDigital) That final program hides inside a normal Windows process, checks for antivirus software, takes desktop screenshots, and keeps a connection open so the operator can send more commands. It also searches for Electrum, Exodus, Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Ledger wallets. Stealers like AMOS are not new on Macs either. A recent AMOS malext malvertising campaign showed the same pattern, with paid ads pushing macOS users toward terminal commands and trojanized Ledger and Trezor apps. Gen’s advice is clear. Never paste a command you did not write yourself, and type the vendor’s address or use a bookmark. Anthropic’s real download page is claude.com/download. Treat the “user-generated” label as a warning sign, and never enter a recovery phrase into software that asks for it unexpectedly. Anyone who already ran one of these commands should assume the device is fully compromised. From a clean device, change important passwords, log out of all sessions, enable multi-factor authentication, and move crypto funds into a wallet created from a new recovery phrase. items.title: Hackers Use Malicious Instagram Ads to Infect iPhones With Spyware Without a Click
items.summary: Hackers are using malicious Instagram advertisements to infect vulnerable iPhones with spyware while users scroll through their feeds. A documented attack used a World Cup advertisement to deliver the P7 variant of DarkSword, exposing sensitive information without requiring the victim to tap the ad, download a file, or install an application. The findings show how online advertising can become a delivery channel for mobile attacks. Unlike phishing, these infections do not depend on persuading someone to open a suspicious link. Earlier reporting on spyware delivered through advertisements documented a separate campaign, highlighting how advertising infrastructure can help attackers reach devices during ordinary browsing. Researchers from iVerify identified the DarkSword P7 infection while investigating an employee’s mobile device at a customer organization. Hackers Use Malicious Instagram Ads Their joint investigation with Report URI , published October 21, 2026, describes criminal groups abusing advertisements and abandoned website integrations to distribute DarkSword and Coruna, two iOS exploit kits capable of stealing private data. In the Instagram case, the employee was simply scrolling when the malicious advertisement loaded. The same person later faced another attack after clicking a malicious link distributed by a different group using another DarkSword variant. Near-real-time alerts allowed the organization’s security team to rotate credentials before stolen login details could be sold and used against corporate systems. The researchers describe these as “half-click” attacks: users must visit a webpage or social platform, but no further interaction with the malicious content is necessary. This distinction matters. The report does not describe an attack that reaches an idle phone without browsing activity, nor does it establish that fully updated iPhones are vulnerable. Polymarket (Source – iVerify) Investigators have not established how the Instagram advertisement passed Meta’s checks. They discuss several possibilities, including concealed malicious content, abuse of advertising resellers, or a compromised vendor. None is confirmed. The observed infection demonstrates an advertising delivery route, not proof of a vulnerability in Instagram itself. The underlying compromise depends on vulnerable iOS software. Previous analysis of Coruna and DarkSword exploits explains how linked browser and system flaws can move an attacker beyond the browser’s safety boundaries. In this investigation, both kits target older iOS versions; placeholders for newer releases do not demonstrate working exploits against them. DeadTag Expands Spyware Delivery Through Forgotten Website Tags Report URI also uncovered DeadTag, an operation that buys expired domains previously used for analytics and advertising services. Thousands of websites still load scripts from those domains through forgotten tags. Once attackers control a domain, those existing connections give them a way to redirect visitors without first compromising each website directly. The researchers identified hundreds of re-registered domains and estimated 135 million monthly visits to sites capable of serving the spyware when visitors meet targeting conditions. That figure measures potential traffic exposure, not confirmed infections. Much of the redirected traffic leads to scams, while selected iPhone visitors receive Coruna or DarkSword. The exploit crew also planted DarkSword loaders on hundreds of PrestaShop stores, hiding them in folders resembling analytics components. Some paths led to a fake Polymarket page. The identified variants targeted keychain passwords, device information, and wallets including Binance, Coinbase Wallet, OKX, Bitget, Trust Wallet, Exodus, TronLink, and Bitpie. The potential damage extends beyond cryptocurrency. Both exploit kits can collect messages, contacts, location information, and passwords. For employers, a compromised personal phone can therefore become a source of corporate credentials, even when the employee never opens a suspicious attachment or knowingly approves an installation. Financial theft appears to be the main motive. Chinese-language code comments and related infrastructure suggest Chinese-speaking operators, but do not establish nationality or state involvement. DeadTag’s operators remain unidentified. Separately, previous reporting on malicious website theme packages shows how browser-side dependencies can expose iPhone visitors to spyware and wallet theft through trusted-looking websites. Users should install available iOS security updates promptly. People facing elevated risk should consider Lockdown Mode, acknowledging its restrictions. Website owners should remove unused third-party tags, monitor external scripts, and enforce a Content Security Policy. Following suspected compromise, the researchers recommend preserving logs before restarting, changing exposed credentials, and replacing affected cryptocurrency wallets with new recovery phrases. items.title: Palo Alto Confirms Brotli Vulnerability Impact on PAN-OS and Releases Workarounds
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that a critical Brotli vulnerability affects some PAN-OS firewall deployments and its Prisma Cloud Application Security Transporter Client. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw could let an attacker corrupt memory, expose sensitive data, crash a service, or potentially run code without authentication. The company published its advisory on October 26, 2026. The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 9.2, although Palo Alto assigns it moderate response urgency. The company says it is not aware of malicious exploitation. Its investigation across products and cloud services remains ongoing, so customers should check the official security advisory for changes to affected versions and patch schedules. Brotli Vulnerability Affects PAN-OS The flaw sits in c/dec/decode.c part of Google’s Brotli decoder. A specially crafted compressed stream can trigger an out-of-bounds write, meaning the decoder writes beyond its intended memory area. Fixed Brotli releases include 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1 for their respective release branches. The same vulnerability also affects other software that uses Brotli. Cybersecurity News previously covered Node.js security updates addressing the decoder flaw and HTTP2Shell research showing its impact beyond web traffic . Those reports show why updating one application may not remove vulnerable copies elsewhere in an organization. For PAN-OS, exposure depends on configuration. PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls must have both Brotli traffic inspection and TLS/SSL decryption enabled on the dataplane, which processes network traffic. The management web interface and API are not affected. Brotli inspection is disabled by default and is unsupported before PAN-OS 11.2.4. PAN-OS 11.1 and 10.2 are unaffected, as are Panorama virtual appliances and M-Series appliances. Administrators running PAN-OS 11.2.4 or later can check the setting with show system setting brotli . An Enabled: yes result confirms Brotli inspection is active, but TLS/SSL decryption must also be enabled for the stated exposure conditions. Workarounds Administrators Can Apply Palo Alto recommends disabling Brotli inspection while awaiting fixes. Through the command-line interface, administrators can run set system setting brotli-encoding disable , then use show system setting brotli to confirm Enabled: no . On PAN-OS 12.1.2 and later, they can instead open Device > Setup > Content-ID, clear Allow Brotli Encoding, and commit the configuration. Threat Prevention subscribers also receive partial coverage through Threat ID 97686 in Applications and Threats content version 9165 or later. This protection is conditional, not a complete fix. The advisory specifies traffic routing, decryption, certificate, and policy requirements for the signature, so customers should not assume installing the content update alone provides protection. The planned PAN-OS fixes span October 27–30. They include 12.2.4-h1, 12.1.4-h13, 12.1.7-h11, 12.1.10-h3, 11.2.4-h23, 11.2.7-h23, 11.2.10-h17, 11.2.13-h4, and 11.2.16-h1. These dates are estimates, not confirmation that every build is available. Notably, 11.2.10-h16 fixes PHP issues only, while 11.2.10-h17 addresses both PHP and Brotli. Prisma Cloud Application Security Transporter Client users should upgrade to version 0.2.9 or later. Palo Alto says listed cloud services, including ADEM, Cloud Identity Engine, Hub, and Prisma AIRS Gateway, have been remediated without customer action. For exposed firewalls, the immediate priority is to disable Brotli inspection, verify the setting, and track the appropriate hotfix for deployment once available. items.title: New Aokigahara Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, and Cursor Login Credentials
items.summary: A newly observed Windows infostealer called Aokigahara is targeting login credentials and session data associated with ChatGPT Desktop, Claude, Codex, and Cursor. The malware searches infected computers for authentication files and application storage, extending familiar password theft into the AI tools developers increasingly use for everyday work. The threat is not evidence that these AI services have been breached. Instead, attackers collect locally stored information that may help them access accounts. Similar AI coding agent theft has shown why tokens, saved connections, and project records deserve the same protection as browser passwords and cloud keys. Researchers from Check Point identified Aokigahara in the wild and detailed its capabilities in an October 23 research report. New Aokigahara Malware They noted that an earlier version may have been known as Kamidere or Stygian, while stressing that the operators’ methods for making money from stolen information remain unconfirmed. A dedicated collection module named aisessions searches for data linked to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, ChatGPT Desktop, and Cursor. Its scope also covers Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, JetBrains AI Assistant, Amazon Q, and Kiro. The module additionally queries Windows Credential Manager for stored credential information. For Claude, collection targets include credential files and desktop application folders. Codex targets include authentication, configuration, and environment files. Cursor’s local storage databases are also selected, while ChatGPT Desktop’s application cache is searched. These locations may contain useful secrets, but not every targeted file necessarily holds a password or token. Earlier reporting on Aoki credential stealing described similar interest in AI application data. The practical risk depends on whether collected secrets remain valid and reusable: working session tokens could give attackers account access without requiring them to enter the victim’s password again. That access could expose private conversations, uploaded material, or development information. Attackers might also consume paid services or resell compromised accounts. Check Point described these as potential outcomes, not confirmed activity by Aokigahara’s operators, and raised possible data extortion where stolen access reveals sensitive business content. A separate ide module widens collection to Git credentials, SSH files that may contain private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud configuration data. Alongside its AI focus, Aokigahara steals browser credentials and cookies, captures screenshots and clipboard contents, and collects wallet, messaging, VPN, and email application data. Evasion, Encrypted Uploads, and Incident Response Aokigahara includes optional checks designed to frustrate malware analysis. Depending on configuration, it examines debugger indicators, virtual machine traces, hardware resources, process counts, and mouse movement. It can also stop running when keyboard or Windows interface language settings match an excluded group, including Russian, Ukrainian, and several regional languages. Its configuration is encrypted with AES-256-CBC and controls which built-in collection modules execute. It also stores server details, communication settings, and fallback destinations. Importantly, disabled collection modules remain embedded in the executable, so the capabilities present in a sample may exceed those enabled during a particular run. The malware packages collected information into ZIP archives, then encrypts uploads using AES-256-GCM. An X25519 key exchange helps establish the encryption key. Separate requests open an upload session, transfer each collection category, and mark completion. The latest analyzed samples use a Windows-looking User-Agent string, although that string alone cannot prove infection. Upload headers identify the collection category and sequence number, allowing the server to separate browser data from AI sessions and other stolen material. The final completion message signals that the upload phase ended; it does not independently confirm that every stolen archive reached the server. The wider trend is already visible in incidents involving a fake Gemini npm package that targeted local data from several AI tools. That separate campaign does not establish Aokigahara’s delivery method; it shows how developer workflows have become attractive places to collect reusable access credentials. For defenders, the collection pattern supports monitoring unexpected processes that read AI authentication stores, editor databases, cloud credentials, and SSH material. Network findings should be checked alongside endpoint evidence rather than treated as standalone proof. Check Point also published a YARA rule to support identification of the malware. After a suspected infection, responders should isolate the device and use a clean system to revoke AI sessions, rotate exposed keys, and review connected cloud and repository accounts. Resetting passwords alone may leave stolen sessions usable. Teams should also review AI account activity and determine whether sensitive conversations or uploaded files were accessible. The findings concern theft from compromised endpoints, not a demonstrated vulnerability in ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, or Cursor. Organizations should therefore include AI application sessions in their existing infostealer response plans rather than treating them as ordinary application settings. items.summary_html:
A newly observed Windows infostealer called Aokigahara is targeting login credentials and session data associated with ChatGPT Desktop, Claude, Codex, and Cursor.

The malware searches infected computers for authentication files and application storage, extending familiar password theft into the AI tools developers increasingly use for everyday work.

The threat is not evidence that these AI services have been breached. Instead, attackers collect locally stored information that may help them access accounts.

Similar AI coding agent theft has shown why tokens, saved connections, and project records deserve the same protection as browser passwords and cloud keys.

Researchers from Check Point identified Aokigahara in the wild and detailed its capabilities in an October 23 research report.

New Aokigahara Malware

They noted that an earlier version may have been known as Kamidere or Stygian, while stressing that the operators’ methods for making money from stolen information remain unconfirmed.

A dedicated collection module named aisessions searches for data linked to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, ChatGPT Desktop, and Cursor.

Its scope also covers Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, JetBrains AI Assistant, Amazon Q, and Kiro. The module additionally queries Windows Credential Manager for stored credential information.

For Claude, collection targets include credential files and desktop application folders. Codex targets include authentication, configuration, and environment files.

Cursor’s local storage databases are also selected, while ChatGPT Desktop’s application cache is searched. These locations may contain useful secrets, but not every targeted file necessarily holds a password or token.

Earlier reporting on Aoki credential stealing described similar interest in AI application data. The practical risk depends on whether collected secrets remain valid and reusable: working session tokens could give attackers account access without requiring them to enter the victim’s password again.

That access could expose private conversations, uploaded material, or development information. Attackers might also consume paid services or resell compromised accounts.

Check Point described these as potential outcomes, not confirmed activity by Aokigahara’s operators, and raised possible data extortion where stolen access reveals sensitive business content.

A separate ide module widens collection to Git credentials, SSH files that may contain private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud configuration data.

Alongside its AI focus, Aokigahara steals browser credentials and cookies, captures screenshots and clipboard contents, and collects wallet, messaging, VPN, and email application data.

Evasion, Encrypted Uploads, and Incident Response

Aokigahara includes optional checks designed to frustrate malware analysis. Depending on configuration, it examines debugger indicators, virtual machine traces, hardware resources, process counts, and mouse movement.

It can also stop running when keyboard or Windows interface language settings match an excluded group, including Russian, Ukrainian, and several regional languages.

Its configuration is encrypted with AES-256-CBC and controls which built-in collection modules execute. It also stores server details, communication settings, and fallback destinations.

Importantly, disabled collection modules remain embedded in the executable, so the capabilities present in a sample may exceed those enabled during a particular run.

The malware packages collected information into ZIP archives, then encrypts uploads using AES-256-GCM. An X25519 key exchange helps establish the encryption key.

Separate requests open an upload session, transfer each collection category, and mark completion. The latest analyzed samples use a Windows-looking User-Agent string, although that string alone cannot prove infection.

Upload headers identify the collection category and sequence number, allowing the server to separate browser data from AI sessions and other stolen material.

The final completion message signals that the upload phase ended; it does not independently confirm that every stolen archive reached the server.

The wider trend is already visible in incidents involving a fake Gemini npm package that targeted local data from several AI tools.

That separate campaign does not establish Aokigahara’s delivery method; it shows how developer workflows have become attractive places to collect reusable access credentials.

For defenders, the collection pattern supports monitoring unexpected processes that read AI authentication stores, editor databases, cloud credentials, and SSH material.

Network findings should be checked alongside endpoint evidence rather than treated as standalone proof. Check Point also published a YARA rule to support identification of the malware.

After a suspected infection, responders should isolate the device and use a clean system to revoke AI sessions, rotate exposed keys, and review connected cloud and repository accounts.

Resetting passwords alone may leave stolen sessions usable. Teams should also review AI account activity and determine whether sensitive conversations or uploaded files were accessible.

The findings concern theft from compromised endpoints, not a demonstrated vulnerability in ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, or Cursor.

Organizations should therefore include AI application sessions in their existing infostealer response plans rather than treating them as ordinary application settings.

items.title: Hackers Sell ICMacOS Remote Access Trojan for $699 a Week to Target Mac Users
items.summary: Cybercriminals are selling a Mac malware kit that can do far more than steal passwords. The tool, called ICMacOS or Icarus macOS, is offered for $699 a week on Russian-speaking dark web forums. It began as a basic data stealer, but its newer version can stay hidden on a Mac, survive restarts, and run commands sent by its operators. SOCRadar’s Threat Research Unit first identified the malware in September 2026 and published a detailed report on October 12. The seller uses the name GlowComa, a financially motivated actor active since January 2026, who promotes the tool under the banner of the MADHASH crypto-draining affiliate group. For more background on how the threat grew, read our detailed ICMacOS evolution report , which explains each change in order. Researchers at Moonlock Lab also noted that ICMacOS is the most affordable macOS stealer sold on the dark web. Moonlock’s write-up, which quotes SOCRadar, compares the price with other Mac threats. AMOS reportedly sells for $3,000 a month, Banshee for $1,500 to $3,000 a month, and MacSync for $1,000 to $1,500 a month. These figures are based on historical reported prices. The seller also has a mixed reputation in the underground market, with several disputes on Exploit.in over poor results and slow service. Hackers Sell ICMacOS Remote Access Trojan The infection starts with fake web pages that trick victims into copying a command and pasting it into Terminal. The command downloads a dropper script that hides the Terminal window and shows a fake System Preferences prompt asking for the login password. The dropper checks that password against the login Keychain and allows up to five tries. It then checks whether the Mac uses Apple Silicon or Intel and downloads the matching payload. This lure style is similar to the fake disk cleanup campaign that Microsoft researchers have tracked since January. The biggest change is in Version 2. It keeps the theft modules but adds a live WebSocket connection to the attacker’s server. Operators can then send commands that run through /bin/sh, and the output returns in real time. The malware also installs a LaunchAgent named com.apple.systemupdater.plist, a name chosen to look like a normal Apple process. It restarts automatically if it stops and runs again every 60 minutes as a backup. Similar tricks have helped other threats get past Apple’s checks, as described in our signed app Gatekeeper bypass coverage. The malware is also built to avoid certain victims. It checks the system language and the victim’s public IP location, and it stops running on systems in Russia and other CIS countries. Its main goal stays the same, which is to steal money and data, but the remote access feature lets criminals stay inside longer. Why Developer Secrets Are at Risk ICMacOS collects a wide range of data. It targets browser passwords and cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, 29 browser extensions, Keychain data, and messaging apps such as Telegram, WhatsApp, and Discord. Developers face the greatest risk because the malware searches for SSH keys, AWS and Kubernetes settings, Git credentials, and .env files. Picus Security’s Umut Bayram warned that one compromised laptop can open a path into a company’s code, cloud systems, and customers. Kevin M. Coles of Coles Technical Group added that developers and executives use Macs often, and those machines hold SSH keys, cloud logins, and crypto wallets. Mac users can lower their risk with a few simple habits. They should never paste commands from a website into Terminal, and they should download software only from verified sources. Apple has added a warning for some risky pasted commands, but it may not catch every case. Anyone who wants to recognize these lures can review our ClickFix Terminal command tricks before running any command. Moonlock sells a Mac security app, so its advice should be read with that in mind, but its tips on checking app privacy policies still apply. Cybercriminals are selling a Mac malware kit that can do far more than steal passwords. The tool, called ICMacOS or Icarus macOS, is offered for $699 a week on Russian-speaking dark web forums.

It began as a basic data stealer, but its newer version can stay hidden on a Mac, survive restarts, and run commands sent by its operators.

SOCRadar’s Threat Research Unit first identified the malware in September 2026 and published a detailed report on October 12.

The seller uses the name GlowComa, a financially motivated actor active since January 2026, who promotes the tool under the banner of the MADHASH crypto-draining affiliate group.

For more background on how the threat grew, read our detailed ICMacOS evolution report, which explains each change in order.

Researchers at Moonlock Lab also noted that ICMacOS is the most affordable macOS stealer sold on the dark web. Moonlock’s write-up, which quotes SOCRadar, compares the price with other Mac threats.

AMOS reportedly sells for $3,000 a month, Banshee for $1,500 to $3,000 a month, and MacSync for $1,000 to $1,500 a month.

These figures are based on historical reported prices. The seller also has a mixed reputation in the underground market, with several disputes on Exploit.in over poor results and slow service.

Hackers Sell ICMacOS Remote Access Trojan

The infection starts with fake web pages that trick victims into copying a command and pasting it into Terminal. The command downloads a dropper script that hides the Terminal window and shows a fake System Preferences prompt asking for the login password.

The dropper checks that password against the login Keychain and allows up to five tries. It then checks whether the Mac uses Apple Silicon or Intel and downloads the matching payload.

This lure style is similar to the fake disk cleanup campaign that Microsoft researchers have tracked since January. The biggest change is in Version 2. It keeps the theft modules but adds a live WebSocket connection to the attacker’s server.

Operators can then send commands that run through /bin/sh, and the output returns in real time. The malware also installs a LaunchAgent named com.apple.systemupdater.plist, a name chosen to look like a normal Apple process.

It restarts automatically if it stops and runs again every 60 minutes as a backup. Similar tricks have helped other threats get past Apple’s checks, as described in our signed app Gatekeeper bypass coverage.

The malware is also built to avoid certain victims. It checks the system language and the victim’s public IP location, and it stops running on systems in Russia and other CIS countries.

Its main goal stays the same, which is to steal money and data, but the remote access feature lets criminals stay inside longer.

Why Developer Secrets Are at Risk

ICMacOS collects a wide range of data. It targets browser passwords and cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, 29 browser extensions, Keychain data, and messaging apps such as Telegram, WhatsApp, and Discord.

Developers face the greatest risk because the malware searches for SSH keys, AWS and Kubernetes settings, Git credentials, and .env files.

Picus Security’s Umut Bayram warned that one compromised laptop can open a path into a company’s code, cloud systems, and customers.

Kevin M. Coles of Coles Technical Group added that developers and executives use Macs often, and those machines hold SSH keys, cloud logins, and crypto wallets.

Mac users can lower their risk with a few simple habits. They should never paste commands from a website into Terminal, and they should download software only from verified sources.

Apple has added a warning for some risky pasted commands, but it may not catch every case. Anyone who wants to recognize these lures can review our ClickFix Terminal command tricks before running any command.

Moonlock sells a Mac security app, so its advice should be read with that in mind, but its tips on checking app privacy policies still apply.

items.title: Claude Code Reportedly Finds 214,856 Deleted Photos and Videos Hidden on Android Phone
items.summary: Anthropic’s Claude Code reportedly found 214,856 files linked to deleted photos and videos on a Google Pixel, raising privacy concerns about Android photos. The user, known as Cooler (@coolerwave), said files remained in a hidden thumbnail folder even after the original images were permanently deleted. This claim is unverified and cannot be confirmed as an Android security flaw. According to a post Cooler (@coolerwave) shared on X, the user connected the Pixel to a MacBook and asked Claude Code to search for leftover media. The tool reportedly identified DCIM/.thumbnails, a hidden folder containing image previews. Claude Code found 214,856 photos and videos I permanently deleted from my Android. Three years of deleted photos and videos still sitting in a hidden cache. Any app with storage access can read them. After the iPhone post I plugged my Pixel into the MacBook and asked Claude… https://t.co/6KCcOJiZ0N pic.twitter.com/14Mksn5deJ — Cooler (@coolerwave) October 25, 2026 Claude Code Finds Deleted Photos Most files were described as compressed copies, while several dozen were said to be close to their original size. The user claimed the files included passport images, bank screenshots, private photographs, and a cryptocurrency seed phrase. The account also said many items were absent from the gallery trash and MediaStore, Android’s media index. However, the material reviewed does not establish that every counted file represented a unique, previously deleted photo or video. The distinction between a cached preview and an original file matters. Android supports loading thumbnails so apps can display smaller previews instead of full media files. Finding a preview would not, by itself, show that Claude Code recovered the original photograph or a playable deleted video. A count of 214,856 files also needs context. A reliable review would need to separate unique images, repeated previews, database files, and other cached content. Without that breakdown, the headline figure should be treated as the user’s reported result, not a verified recovery total. The story follows another reported AI discovery covered by Cyber Security News, in which Claude identified a suspected hidden cryptocurrency miner on a Mac . Such reports show interest in AI-assisted checks, but individual findings still need independent validation.

The post’s claim that any app with storage access can read every deleted image is too broad. Android’s scoped storage rules limit file access, with scoped storage required for apps targeting Android 11 or higher.

Actual access depends on the Android version, app permissions, and file location. Android 14 also introduced selected photo access, allowing users to share specific images rather than their entire library.

Separately, the special MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE permission grants broad access to shared storage, but does not unlock other apps’ protected directories. Ordinary photo permission and “All files access” are therefore not interchangeable.

That distinction matters because excessive permissions can create real risks. Cyber Security News previously covered Android spyware posing as WhatsApp and Google Photos, which used granted privileges to support surveillance and data theft.

Users should review photo permissions and special all-files access, removing access that does not match an app’s purpose. Selected-photo sharing offers a narrower option where supported. Cloud copies need separate attention. Google explains that its “Free up space” feature removes local copies while keeping backed-up images available in Google Photos.

items.title: Apache Camel Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities Including High-Severity XXE One’s
items.summary: Apache Camel has released fixes for multiple security flaws, including high-severity XML External Entity vulnerabilities that could expose local files or reach internal systems. The issues affect several components, with risks ranging from unsafe XML processing to remote code execution, stolen credentials, and failed access checks. Apache’s security advisories list patched releases for each affected branch. The fixes cover different parts of Camel, so exposure depends on the components and settings an application uses. Teams should check their deployed versions against the individual advisories rather than assume every Camel application faces the same risk. Several flaws require attacker-controlled messages to reach a specific processing path. One significant issue, CVE-2026-90885, affects Camel-Saxon. Its XQueryBuilder processed message bodies already represented as javax.xml.transform.Source objects using Saxon’s default parser settings. This allowed an external entity declared inside the XML body to be resolved, creating an XXE weakness in that processing path. According to Apache’s Camel-Saxon advisory, this issue is separate from CVE-2026-85250 in Camel-XPath. The XPath flaw appears when documentType=InputSource passes the payload to an engine that builds its own parser using JDK defaults. XML declarations blocked by the default document type could therefore be accepted through this alternative path. Apache Camel Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities A third high-severity issue, CVE-2026-88901, affects Camel-Smooks. Its default XML reader resolved external general and parameter entities and loaded external document type definitions. An attacker-controlled XML message could consequently read local files or contact internal hosts. Camel-FOP also received a medium-severity XXE fix for unsafe handling when certain third-party XML transformer implementations were present. The broader update includes CVE-2026-88900, a high-severity unsafe Java deserialization flaw in Camel-JGroups that can lead to remote code execution. Another high-severity issue, CVE-2026-78165, affects Camel-Spring-Redis. An attacker who can publish to a subscribed channel could exploit its default deserializer, which lacks an object input filter. Camel-HTTP also contains a high-severity credential disclosure issue tracked as CVE-2026-85251. When followRedirects was enabled, the component attached the Authorization header to the destination named by a redirect, allowing a remote server to choose where those credentials were sent. Other fixes address OAuth authentication bypass and Keycloak token validation weaknesses. These findings follow earlier coverage of Apache Camel header injection and attacks targeting Tomcat and Camel vulnerabilities . Those reports concern older flaws and should not be treated as evidence that the newly listed issues are being exploited. For the Saxon flaw, Apache lists fixes in versions 4.18.5, 4.22.2, and 4.23.0. Apache fixed the XPath and Smooks issues in 4.18.5, 4.22.1, and 4.23.0. Organizations choosing an upgrade should account for the later Saxon fix rather than stop at 4.22.1. Review deployed XML components, message entry points, and redirect settings during patch planning. Use Apache’s component-specific version ranges to confirm coverage, especially where multiple Camel libraries are packaged within one application. items.title: New DarkCore RAT Targets Gmail and WhatsApp Sessions While Hiding Behind Victims’ IP Addresses
items.summary: A newly uncovered remote access trojan called DarkCore is being marketed with a browser designed to reuse stolen Gmail, WhatsApp, and other account sessions while routing traffic through victims’ IP addresses. The approach could make unauthorized account access look like normal activity from an already trusted connection. The Windows malware combines advertised credential theft, file transfers, a reverse proxy, and hidden desktop access. However, researchers drew an important line between the seller’s claims and confirmed code behavior: their analysis established the client’s configuration and module loading, but did not independently verify every advertised browser feature. Researchers from BlackFog identified DarkCore during routine threat hunting and examined a marketplace listing dated August 11, 2026. Their published technical malware analysis compared promotional screenshots with a supplied Windows executable and an accompanying malicious shortcut. A screenshot contained 118 credential rows, but that figure does not establish how many victims were compromised. New DarkCore RAT Targets Gmail and WhatsApp Sessions Session cookies represent a login that has already succeeded. Instead of entering a password and completing another authentication challenge, an attacker may reuse a valid stolen session. Earlier reporting on Cookie-Bite session theft attacks explains the same broader risk: stealing authenticated cookies can undermine protections applied during login. DarkCore’s marketplace listing (Source – Blackfog) DarkCore’s seller showed Gmail, WhatsApp, YouTube, and MediaFire inside its dedicated browser. According to the advertised changelog, operators can inject stolen cookies and send browser traffic through the infected device’s IP address. The proxy reportedly stops when the last browser window associated with that session closes. These remain seller-described functions rather than fully validated findings. The distinction matters because a familiar IP address does not prove that the legitimate user controls an account. Victim-IP routing is intended to disguise unauthorized access as ordinary browsing. Investigators therefore need to connect account activity with endpoint evidence rather than treating a recognized network address as sufficient reassurance. DarkCore’s browser and service list, with private content redacted (Source – Blackfog) DarkCore also advertises hidden virtual network computing, or HVNC, which lets an operator control a browser on a Windows desktop the victim cannot see. Similar MedusaHVNC hidden desktop capabilities illustrate how attackers can work inside existing browser sessions without changing the visible desktop. DarkCore’s promotional interface showed Chrome open on Gmail. PDF Shortcut Delivery and Technical Findings The accompanying shortcut uses a PDF icon and presents itself as a report launcher. Opening it starts a minimized command window that downloads a genuine World Bank report as a decoy and separately retrieves an executable. String slicing, character removal, and CALL expansion conceal the underlying download and launch commands. Before opening either download, the commands attempt to remove its Zone.Identifier stream, the Windows marker associated with internet downloads. This can reduce warnings. The executable download is attempted even if the decoy PDF fails, and its launch command does not check whether retrieval succeeded. How attackers originally distributed the shortcut remains unknown. This resembles PDF decoy delivery techniques reported in another RAT campaign, where a document distracts the user while malicious code runs. Gmail displayed through DarkCore’s HVNC interface (Source – Blackfog) BlackFog could not hash the remotely hosted executable, so it could not confirm that the download matched the supplied sample it examined. That sample was an unsigned, 64-bit Windows executable. Researchers recovered its settings by reproducing a decoder that rotates bytes from a 32-byte key and XORs them against 758 encoded bytes. The configuration selected direct TCP communication, disabled Tor and WebSocket options, and left installation and startup persistence flags unset. Additional modules can load directly into memory or through temporary DLL files written to disk. For detection, BlackFog recommends examining command-shell downloads, process ancestry, file signatures, and network connections together. If theft is suspected, responders should isolate the endpoint, preserve evidence, stop unauthorized transfers, revoke active sessions, and reset affected credentials. items.title: Hackers Can Abuse Logged-In WordPress Admin Sessions to Secretly Install PHP Backdoors
items.summary: WordPress administrators often keep their dashboard open in the same browser they use for everyday browsing. A new attack chain shows why that habit is risky. Researchers have documented a JavaScript loader that waits for a signed-in administrator to visit a compromised page, then uses that browser’s trusted session to install a hidden PHP backdoor on the website. The attacker never needs the admin password, because the administrator’s own browser does the work. Recent cases point to the same pattern. One example is an admin-triggered WordPress malware campaign that exposed more than 1.2 million websites to potential compromise. Malware that activates only during logged-in sessions is hard to spot during routine scans, which makes it a growing concern for site owners. Security researchers at Securonix Threat Research, Akshay Gaikwad and Aaron Beardslee, identified the malware and named the chain TRUST#GRAFT. Their analysis shows that the JavaScript does not break the WordPress login. Instead, it checks whether the visitor is already signed in as an administrator, then reuses that session to add new code to the site. Securonix also notes that it has not confirmed how the first script reached the compromised page. Hackers Can Abuse Logged-In WordPress Admin Sessions The infection begins with a fake security check. The script places a full-screen frame over the page that looks like a Cloudflare “Just a moment” verification screen. While the visitor waits, the script collects details such as screen size, graphics data, timezone, and installed plugin count. It also checks for signs of automated analysis tools. After solving a small puzzle, the browser sends this data to a controller server, which decides whether to send the next stage. The key step follows. The script requests the WordPress plugin upload page using the browser’s existing login cookies, then reads a WordPress security token, called a nonce, from that page. Researchers have documented a JavaScript loader that waits for a signed-in administrator to visit a compromised page, then uses that browser’s trusted session to install a hidden PHP backdoor on the website.

The attacker never needs the admin password, because the administrator’s own browser does the work. Recent cases point to the same pattern.

One example is an admin-triggered WordPress malware campaign that exposed more than 1.2 million websites to potential compromise.

Malware that activates only during logged-in sessions is hard to spot during routine scans, which makes it a growing concern for site owners.

Security researchers at Securonix Threat Research, Akshay Gaikwad and Aaron Beardslee, identified the malware and named the chain TRUST#GRAFT.

Their analysis shows that the JavaScript does not break the WordPress login. Instead, it checks whether the visitor is already signed in as an administrator, then reuses that session to add new code to the site. Securonix also notes that it has not confirmed how the first script reached the compromised page.

While the visitor waits, the script collects details such as screen size, graphics data, timezone, and installed plugin count. It also checks for signs of automated analysis tools.

After solving a small puzzle, the browser sends this data to a controller server, which decides whether to send the next stage. The key step follows.

items.summary: Hackers have revived techniques associated with the BlackLotus bootkit to bypass Windows Secure Boot and deploy espionage malware against diplomatic organizations in Central Asia. The new bootkit, named BlackX, appeared in attacks targeting agencies in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan in early 2026. Investigators linked the campaign to APT41 with medium confidence, leaving attribution short of confirmation. The finding was not simply another case of missing security updates. Investigators found that affected computers were fully patched, but vulnerable boot components remained trusted because additional certificate revocation steps had not been completed. Earlier reporting on Windows boot manager downgrades explains how older, signed components can undermine protections on otherwise updated systems. Researchers from Securelist identified BlackX during their investigation and detailed its operation in an October 22 technical report. Hackers Revive BlackLotus Techniques Kaspersky researchers Georgy Kucherin, Vladimir Nestor, and Vasily Berdnikov found that its exploitation chain closely resembles BlackLotus, although its implementation and later payloads differ. BlackX exploits Baton Drop, tracked as CVE-2022-21894, to manipulate the startup trust chain. Attackers deploy it after compromising a network and obtaining administrator privileges. It is therefore a tool for extending an existing compromise, rather than the initial route into a victim’s environment. The report does not establish how those networks were first breached. Installation separates the executable from an encrypted package containing the required components and strings. This arrangement leaves the installer without embedded malicious payloads, making recovery and analysis harder when responders cannot retrieve its companion file. BlackLotus advertisement (Source – Securelist) The package writes components to system and UEFI partitions, then exploits Baton Drop to install custom Machine Owner Keys. These keys enable attacker-controlled EFI files to load. The bootkit subsequently injects a signed malicious driver into the Windows kernel. Its signing certificate has since been revoked. The driver attempts to disable security callbacks and interfere with Event Tracing for Windows providers, reducing visibility into malicious activity. However, researchers found that its Kaspersky-specific interference routines failed during testing. It also redirects requests for protected bootkit files toward a harmless Windows executable. Espionage Payloads and the Secure Boot Protection Gap BlackX delivers two observed user-mode payloads. One is a remote-access Trojan capable of loading additional .NET code and exchanging instructions through Google Drive, OneDrive, or Yandex.Disk. Similar Google Drive command channels have appeared in separate APT41-linked reporting, illustrating how trusted cloud platforms can carry attacker instructions alongside ordinary business traffic. This similarity alone does not prove attribution. The second payload, OxiDLLRunner, uses an obfuscated DLL loaded through a legitimate executable. It decrypts a nearby data file containing shellcode and a Rust executable. That payload contacts command infrastructure and receives additional DLL plugins, which execute in separate threads. The design gives operators a way to extend functionality after establishing access. Researchers based their APT41 assessment on shared development identifiers, overlaps with previously reported FishMonger activity, DLL sideloading patterns, and OLLVM obfuscation. These clues support their medium-confidence judgment, but do not establish who wrote BlackX. They suggested its developers might have reverse-engineered BlackLotus or purchased its source code; neither explanation was confirmed. The protection gap involved continued trust in vulnerable components signed under Windows Production PCA 2011. Securelist reported that installing updates did not automatically activate the required revocation on affected systems. Certificate expiration on October 19 also did not independently block existing binaries. Microsoft’s certificate expiration advisory likewise explains that existing devices continue starting normally after expiration. Administrators should verify boot-trust revocations rather than relying only on update status. Previous UEFI Secure Boot vulnerabilities demonstrate why forbidden-signature databases matter. Revocation changes require compatibility planning because older recovery media and boot configurations may depend on certificates being removed.
